children.translated_text: First Inquiry
To him who has pacified all obstacles,
through the removal of the serpent of pride,
who is the treasury of truth and nectar,
who shines forth by his own light,
who is the opposite of <s>saṃsāra</s> (worldly existence),
whose arrogance of mind has been removed,
who sprinkles the nectar of tranquility —
to <s>Viveka</s> (Discernment), salutation upon salutation!
(A couplet)
<s>Kṣemendra</s>, out of love for his friends,
as a physician for the disease of pride,
strives for [their] health
with the sweet medicines of well-spoken sayings.
Lineage, wealth, learning, beauty,
valor, generosity, and austerity —
these seven are, predominantly,
the causes of intoxication among human beings.
For the benefit of embodied beings
overpowered by ego, as if by evil spirits,
this Crushing of Pride is composed
for the pacification of delusion.
Of those who reckon 'lineage! lineage!'
deluded by false pride —
'We do not know what this [spirit] is that has seized them,
this demon that stiffens their necks!'
If the root of lineage, like that of a lotus,
is sought out,
then inevitably it is revealed to be
immersed in the mud of faults.
Just as from a thoroughbred horse
a true thoroughbred cannot [always] be born,
so the son of a virtuous man,
born of that very family, may be devoid of virtues.
If one ancestor in the family
was a performer of sacrifices and greatly learned,
while another was a sinful fool —
whose lineage does the family follow?
In the world, lineage remains lineage only
as long as the continuity with ancestors persists;
when the power of virtues is severed,
the entire lineage is finished.
What pride of lineage can those have
who are born from the lowest origins —
those whose mothers are women
who overflow the banks of family like lowland rivers?
'Of good family! Of good family!' —
ashamed by the newness of poverty,
what use is lineage before a non-kinsman
when one babbles pitifully in begging?
Even one born in a virtuous family,
if devoid of virtues — by whom is he honored?
A cow born in a line of milch-cows,
if barren — of what use is she to anyone?
One makes one's own lineage; therefore,
having reflected, let pride be abandoned.
Knowing that lineage depends on virtues,
let the mind be devoted to virtues.
When one searches for the root, upon constant reflection there is truly no lineage of men,
for it is women through whom the chain of progeny extends in succession;
before these women — accomplished in the artifice of concealment, possessed of modesty —
who truly knows the deep and hidden conduct of their firmly rooted, secret passions?
The mother of one who is adorned with pride of lineage,
or the grandmother, or the great-grandmother —
if she was corrupted by the nature of womankind,
then this is the fault that strikes at the very root of the family.
In the Solar dynasty, <s>Triśaṅku</s>,
a <s>caṇḍāla</s> (outcast), became a king;
<s>Dilīpa</s>, <s>Raghu</s>, <s>Rāma</s>, and others,
all those kings were born of that very lineage.
Of the kings of the Lunar dynasty,
the progenitor was <s>Budha</s> (Mercury) —
he was born from the Moon's
transgression upon the teacher's bed, as is well known in the world.
<s>Karṇa</s> was the son of an unmarried girl;
the sons of <s>Pāṇḍu</s> were <s>kṣetraja</s> (field-born);
what purpose is served by further
common discussions about lineage?
In <s>Mathurā</s>, there once lived
a <s>brāhmaṇa</s>, the best among the prosperous,
a performer of sacrifices named <s>Śrutanidhi</s>,
learned, of renowned learning.
He had a beloved wife
named <s>Muktālatā</s>, born of a tall lineage,
who was his darling spouse,
of graceful form endowed with beauty.
In her, by him, was born a handsome
son of excellent conduct, foremost in virtues,
named <s>Tejonidhi</s>,
a spotless mirror of learning.
He, the wise one — Veda-learned, eloquent,
a poet, the abode of all arts —
in the assemblies of the learned, caused
heads to bow in shame.
Him, fevered with the disease of pride,
afflicted with stiffness of the neck,
the father, out of affection, in private,
began to speak wholesome [words] for his pacification.
'O son, with false pride
why have you descended into foolishness —
you who, mounted on the elephant of arrogance,
feel ashamed of honoring those worthy of honor?
There is no remedy in this world
for those fools who, falling from the precipice of pride,
by which even a moment's
support by the hand can be given.
Alas! By whom were you taught —
you whose memory of good conduct has been destroyed —
this intoxication arising from lineage, learning, and wealth,
that has entered [even] among good people?
The connection of lineage is unstable;
learning is always contentious;
intoxication leads only to delusion;
and wealth is but a death lasting a moment.
This alone is nobility of birth,
this alone is the acquisition of virtues —
that always, among the good, before the virtuous,
the head is bowed in humility.
Compassion alone is true learning;
truth alone is imperishable wealth;
for those of unblemished discernment,
good character alone is the spotless lineage.
Prosperity beautiful even without enjoyment,
lineage bright without servility,
learning clear without pride —
these belong to the noble-minded.
Whose hatred does not lead to harm?
Whose affection does not lead to prosperity?
Whose pride does not lead to downfall?
And whose humility does not lead to elevation?
What use is a generous man who is poor?
What use is a man of noble birth who is sinful?
What use is a contented man who is miserly?
What use is a wise man blinded by pride?
Friendship turns to enmity;
giving turns to taking;
for one possessed by the demon of pride,
learning turns into a hundredfold folly.
Jealousy is the enemy of the virtuous;
the excessive beggar is the enemy of the greedy;
everyone is the enemy of the proud,
but no one is the enemy of those who speak kindly.
Therefore, O son, you must never
cultivate egotism;
for one whose neck is raised with pride is soon
seized by the crocodile of delusion.
From lineage endowed with eminence, from a host of inner qualities that cause wonder,
from beauty that is exceedingly captivating, from great wealth or [noble] conduct —
the great tree of delusion, made of intoxication, always grows;
your effort must be directed first at uprooting its deeply established roots.
O son, even having attained prosperity,
do not show disregard for virtues;
even a full pot, [when drawn] from a well,
falls down if the rope (<s>guṇa</s>) is cut.
Abandon pride of lineage — it is concealed at the top;
abandon pride of wealth — it is seen and then lost;
abandon pride of learning — it is a mere commodity;
abandon pride of beauty — it is licked away by time.
O son, you have been carefully awakened;
if you do not relinquish the delusion of pride,
then this conceit, which generates intense suffering,
will become a thorn [lodged] within you.'
The elephant in the lotus-pond of prosperity, the thunderbolt that shatters the honor of good people,
the guide to the path of downfall, the smoke that rises from the painting of merit,
the fever of sleeping on another's bed, the cloud over the moon of good conduct —
intoxication is always the cause of the destruction of virtues for those of proud minds.
If this impermanence were permanence,

children.text: sarvaṃ na pāke virasaṃ yadi syāt
children.translated_text: if everything did not become tasteless in its ripening,
then this pride born of lineage, wealth, learning, and the rest
would not be something to be mocked.
'I am the debater, the weighty master of learning among all scholars;
I am the honored one, a great poet through the maturation of the flow of speech;
I am the playful swan, dwelling in the hearts of lotus-eyed women' —
thus the demon of intoxication makes its acquaintance within men.
<s>Lakṣmī</s> (Prosperity) perishes in a moment, even when guarded;
the body is but a collection of decays;
the happy conjunction of enjoyment and union is itself unreal —
this is the curse: the dense cloud of false pride.
Though admonished repeatedly by his father,
with eyes playfully half-closed,
he went off like a maddened elephant
impetuously disregarding the goad.
They scratch the ground with their feet, intoxicated, breathing hot breaths of anger,
they make their faces terrible with frowning brows through oblique, sidelong glances,
with their foreheads' skin wearied by the rubbing of perspiring finger-stalks —
they tremble when salutary counsel is spoken, as if possessed by evil spirits.
He once, when fine horses were standing ready
for the sport of racing,
set out riding a donkey
to a friend's house for a festival.
Goaded by him with a sharp prod
again and again,
the donkey was afflicted by intense pain,
drenched with flowing blood from its wounds.
With tearful eyes, declaring its distress
in the language of its own species' call,
it spoke to a she-donkey, its own mother,
who had come before it.
'O mother, this son of a <s>brāhmaṇa</s>,
look at me — this vile-minded one —
tearing me with his goad,
is intent on killing me as I carry him!
What shall I do? For I was obtained
by this wicked soul [somehow] —
shall I throw him into a ditch
or hurl [my] body into a pit?'
To her son crying in distress,
the she-donkey, with tearful eyes,
spoke to him with great sorrow,
her suffering spreading through her affection:
'Bear this ill-mannered one, O son,
endure the terrible pain;
in the heart of this cruel one
there is not even a grain of compassion.
This fierce one was born of a <s>śūdra</s>
in a <s>brāhmaṇa</s> woman, devoid of <s>Brahman</s>;
he does not know the suffering of others,
violent in his <s>caṇḍāla</s>-like behavior.
A heart impoverished of compassion,
speech harsh as a saw —
this is the visible mark
of those born of mixed castes.
Speech soft as fresh butter,
a heart tender with compassion,
a head bowed in humility —
these belong to those born from a single seed.
He cries out harshly with fierce bluster, hostile without cause through anger,

children.text: spṛśati na dayāṃ dainyāpanne vijātitayā śaṭhaḥ
children.translated_text: does not touch compassion for one fallen into misery — the rogue, because of his mixed birth,
fickle as sand for a moment, he despises those who serve him,
the villain with his swollen throat makes belches of arrogance toward the virtuous.'
Hearing these unbearable words
of the she-donkey, the twice-born one,
who understood the speech of all creatures,
fell down, struck by bewilderment.
He, having regained consciousness after a long time,
as if fallen from the peak of <s>Meru</s>,
suddenly abandoned his pride,
all his family's eminence destroyed.
As if stupefied by poison,
he went to his mother's side
and, having reported what he had heard,
questioned her in private about everything.
Pressed by him who was ready to abandon his body,
adjured by him, she,
with downcast face, told him
in words faltering with embarrassment:
'How shall I tell you this
shameful, wicked deed?
More impenetrable than <s>saṃsāra</s> itself,
and more astonishing, is the conduct of women.
More than the tip of an elephant's ear,
more than a leaf of the <s>pippala</s> tree,
more than the flashing of lightning —
fickle is the mind of a woman.
They are not restrained by the virtues of a husband,
they are not detected by those who watch,
they are not prevented by wealth —
women who are bent on abandoning chastity.
Swept away by the flood of passion's turbidity
born of wealth and youth,
who can restrain women — fallen from the heights,
flowing downward like rivers?
Givers of the body, takers of men's lives;
timid by nature, they enter fire;
cruel, yet with limbs delicate as petals —
appearing innocent, they deceive even the clever.
I once, bathed in the dust [of springtime],
in the season marked by blossoms,
alone in the flower garden,
stood maddened by youth.
My husband being absorbed in the observance of a vow,
with downcast face as if from jealousy,
with hands placed on my high breasts,
I pondered for a long time.
These creepers, trembling with the wind's sighs,
with their yawning [blossoms], to the sound of bees,
sing as if with longing —
the creepers laden with the pollen of flowers.
Overcome by the onslaught of budding youth,
separated from the enjoyment of my beloved,
I am rendered fruitless
by the fault of my husband, devoted to the remainder of his vow.
At that moment of reflection,
holding a mirror before his face,
a barber named <s>Parihāsa</s> (Jest)
arrived, like an enemy of chastity.
Seeing me alone,
frightened and with composure lost,
he touched me — trembling —
in the play of grasping my foot-nails.
There, I — with my duty abandoned,
ashamed of the contact with a low person,
with downcast face, as if watching
my fallen virtue — swooned.
That she-donkey, roaming nearby,
saw all of this;
and this deed, which gave rise to a secret pregnancy,
is my sin against my family.
Enough, O son, with this discussion
of hidden affairs;
concealed bodies and concealed [reputations of] families alone
are resplendent.'
Hearing his mother's words,
he was suddenly plunged into blindness;
from the downfall of his pride in birth,
he became as if lifeless.
Then, fasting, he went
to <s>Kailāsa</s>, laughing at [worldly delusion],
and, with his hopes fixed on <s>brāhmaṇya</s> (Brahminhood),
he practiced austerity for a very long time.
Pleased by his fierce austerity,
<s>Śatakratu</s> (<s>Indra</s>) himself
did not grant <s>brāhmaṇya</s> (Brahminhood) to him who sought it,
for it is unattainable on earth.
Again and again, having scorched the three worlds
with his austerity,
he obtained from the boon of the thousand-eyed one (<s>Indra</s>)
godhood, but not the status of a <s>brāhmaṇa</s>.
Then, under the name <s>Chandodeva</s>,
he became renowned on earth —
to be worshipped on one day each year
by doe-eyed women.
A great serpent is this pride of birth and caste, [leading into] the abyss of delusion;
therefore, pride of birth and lineage should not be indulged.
Those who take refuge in tranquility, forbearance, generosity, and compassion —
they consider noble character as [their] expansive lineage.
He whose mother is not the mass of ignorance,
whose father is not the ocean of rebirth,
whose beloved is not clinging desire —
he alone in the world is accomplished and noble-born.
Second Inquiry
What is this pride of men arising from wealth,
which is as fickle as the sidelong glance of <s>Lakṣmī</s>'s eye?
even if bound to one's neck, does not follow
a single step behind one who has passed away.
Well-guarded, it remains without cause;
unguarded, it remains by the conjunction of fate.
The wealth of a miser, whether hoarded or employed,
is like the dance of a madman.
By the fabrication of business-talk and jests,
of those who rush about every morning
[crying] 'Wealth! Wealth!' and prattling on,
death is forgotten by men.
Of the lustreless and the spendthrift,
both distressed by the triple misery of hardship,
what difference is there in the fault of affliction
between the miser and the pauper?
Those who are armored in the acquisition of wealth
and do not see the limit of death —
while they condemn greed,
others enjoy their wealth in the end.
When spoken of, [the wealth of the rich] becomes prey for others;
when unspoken of, it vanishes into invisibility;
it lodges in the heart like a thorn —
such is the wealth of the wealthy at [their] death.
With his wealth, as with his life,
stuck in his throat, the afflicted one gazes
at the faces of his kinsmen
even at the end, with [wealth] still concealed.
That which was earned through great hardship,
earned yet never enjoyed,
that which is divided by another in the end —
let no one have such wealth!
Learning [leads] to disputation, wealth to intoxication,
excellence of intellect to the deception of others,
extreme eminence to the humiliation of the world —
for those whose light is [actually] darkness.
With unquenched inner thirst increased by the brackish water of bits of wealth,
with a body that has lost its luster through long, joyless, and harsh eating,
with sleeplessness, weak digestion, and fear of kings, water, thieves, and fire —
the misery of misers is clearly worse than the misery of the destitute.
In <s>Śrāvastī</s> there was a caravan-leader,
like another lord of wealth (<s>Kubera</s>),
named <s>Nanda</s> — [yet] joyless,
even at the mere mention [of his name] by supplicants.
That miser, always unbearably distressing
to all people,
sleeping atop his hoards,
was like the serpent of Time.
Having spent the entire day
in the procedure of counting the pots of his hoards,
he would eat at night, accustomed to measuring out parched grain,
his belly racked with cramps.
Without condiments, without salt, ruined,
with unrefined cooking, lodged in wretchedness,
never seeing laughter due to the suppression of expenditure —
his house was mute with grief.
Lustreless, devoid of comfort and joy,
without lamps, without water —
the house of that wretched miser
was like the other world [the realm of the dead].
He, always [occupied with] the accumulation of provisions
yet never eating, afflicted with constant ailments,
though possessing gold was pale,
though full [of wealth] was emaciated with worry.
A [woman] named <s>Mati</s> (Intellect), who is obtained through merit,
like the embodiment of the prosperity of wealth,
became the wife — by a reversal of fate —
of that undeserving man.
She always secretly
performed hospitality toward guests on behalf of her husband,
[but] by him, through quarrels over expenditure,
she was withered by the fire of conflict.
From her, his son was born,
virtuous and named <s>Candana</s> (Sandalwood),
[but] by his father, blinded by greed,
he was led into otherness, like a lotus [in darkness].
Once, at the door of his own house,
seeing a supplicant who had obtained food,
<s>Nanda</s> made a quarrel with his wife
[even] to the point of drawing blood.
He spoke, his lip bitten with anger,
hissing at his downcast wife
who was, as it were, washing from her breasts with tears
the sin of his touch.
'Who will give alms to me,
whose wealth is diminished by your hand?
You who are the mother of poverty
stand in this house, O wretched woman!'
'Where women become bold,
concealing the authority of the husband,
that house inevitably becomes
the abode of the greatest calamities.'
'The householder has one house,
but the supplicant has a hundred houses.',
'When wealth is roasted away by a wife,
the householder's course is lost.'
'Wealth, which gives satisfaction even by [mere] sight,
which is the very life of life for a being —
those who protect it
devour their own bodies.'
'A pauper, though living, is inactive [like a corpse];
a corpse, through wealth, is active.',
'Poverty is death in this world;
wealth is the life-span of the embodied.'
'This very power of wealth
is perceived directly —
that a corpse is carried on a bier
by the living who are yoked to the burden.'
'Why do you give food to supplicants —
food accumulated through hardship?
What is given, they say, is for the sake of gaining —
then why is what is gained not protected?'
'The bond of sons, wives, and others
among men depends on wealth.',
'When it is diminished, sons flee
and wives go elsewhere.'
'Scholars, poets, heroes,
artists, ascetics —
like [patients looking at] a physician, [all] look
with afflicted faces at the one who has wealth.'
Having heard those words of the wretched man,
merciless regarding wealth,
she spoke to him what was fitting
for [one of] noble character and good birth:
'The virtuous earn wealth with effort
for the sake of <s>dharma</s> (righteousness).',
'For those who are not disciplined in righteous conduct,
wealth is [merely] an accumulation of impurity.'
'That which produces distaste, suffering,
craving, delusion, and sleeplessness —
that is not the wealth of misers;
it is indeed a disease of the heart.'
'The disease of wealth that grows,
causing separation from the enjoyment of happiness —
its path of quick remedy
is through the treatment of kings and physicians.'
'In whose house, due to greed,
there was never any festival —
at his death, the inheritors of his wealth
dance with drums.'
'You carefully guard the chaff, husks, and embers,
[yet] you do not see
the heap of jewels in the treasury
carried away by mice.'
'What pride, pray, comes from wealth
that perishes in an instant,
consumed by expenditure even when guarded,
devoured by calamities?'
'When examined in truth,
since men's [fortunes] are subject to fate,
in no condition whatsoever
is the greed for wealth praiseworthy.'
'In the <s>Kali</s> age, with wicked friends,
with a son given to vice,
with thieves on the increase,
with a greedy king — what use is wealth?'
'For one [beset] by creditors' quarrels constantly,
whose good qualities find no unbroken path,
who hates giving, who is childless,
and whose digestion is weak — what use is wealth?'
'For one who has suddenly acquired wealth
through treason against the king and such crimes,
who out of fear never spends —
what use is wealth, [which is] like a thorn?'
'For one seized by the terrible [sin of] accepting
gifts from villages, whose lofty virtues and vigor are swallowed up,
who knows not the proper distribution [of wealth],
who has obtained [it] from rogues — what use is wealth?'
'For one exhausted by night-service,
standing in cold, wind, and heat,
delighted by the master's glance,
deserving of hardship — what use is wealth?'
'For one who, out of greed for abundant gain,
has invested wealth everywhere,
who is satisfied by seeing [only] birch-bark [records],
whose judgment is lost — what use is wealth?'
'For a merchant of filthy habits,
spat upon with disgust,
who is [avoided] like the cooking-smell
of impure garlic — what use is wealth?'
'For one who, though desirous, has not obtained [wealth]
during youth, the age worthy of enjoyment,
whose body is worn out by old age —
what use is wealth, [which is] like a burden?'
'For one who has renounced his home
yet, through the reverence and worship of people,
has accumulated wealth —
what use is wealth, [which is] like a fetter?'
'For a youth devoid of the goad [of wisdom],
led astray by rogues,
whose [wealth is] used up in momentary pleasures —
what use is wealth, [which is] like a dream?'
'For an official stationed in a village
whose wife goes about freely —
wealth that is forcibly enjoyed [by others]
and obtained through sin — what use is such wealth?'
'For a guru whose complete enjoyments —
pleasures, garments, and other affluences —
are provided by disciples, and who has succeeded through pretense,
what use is accumulated wealth?'
'For one appointed over the royal treasury,
who bears only the mark of theft,
whose every expenditure is suspect —
what use is wealth, [which is] like death?'
'For an astrologer, whose [wealth is] always perishing
through unforeseen future calamities such as theft,
and who is the sole cause of ridicule in the world —
what use is wealth?'
'For a villager who, like a full sack,
is to be squeezed by the king,
who eats [only] vegetables cooked without [proper] ingredients —
what use is wealth?'
'For a scribe consumed by the pen's [work],
black with ink, an enjoyer [only in name],
who at the end faces imminent imprisonment —
what use is wealth?'
'For one tormented by violent quarrels with his wife,
who constantly [endures] neglect like grass,
scorched by the anger, fasting, and sighs
[of his wife] — what use is wealth?'
'For a miser who is dirty, wearing rags,
devoted to eating little,
whose wretchedness exceeds that of poverty —
what use is wealth?'
'The wealthy are seen to be unhappy;
the wealthy are exceedingly miserable.',
'Since the arising of happiness and sorrow for a being
is subject to fate — what use is wealth?'
'When equals have passed away,
when one's own people are empty of heart,
when one is disenchanted with the joyless, wearisome <s>saṃsāra</s> (worldly existence) —
what use is wealth?'
'For a wise man who uses wealth as it comes,
who is free from anxiety,
contented with very little,
who is satisfied — what use is [more] wealth?'
'A child looks equally at grass and gold,
knowing no preference, with undiscriminating mind.',
'With wealth that is able to fill a treasury, at that age
when one is devoid of discernment — tell me, what does one do?'
'When, upon the sudden separation from a friend dearer than life,
or from a young woman, or from a son who is a treasury of virtues,
the embodied one grieves helplessly with sorrow —
tell me, what does one do then, even with mountains of jewels?'

children.text: nārthaṃ śṛṇoti na punaḥ sthitimīhate vā
children.translated_text: 'One hears no meaning, nor desires stability,

children.text: sparśaṃ na vetti na rasaṃ na tathādhivāsam
children.translated_text: perceives no touch, no taste, no fragrance.',
'When an old man is reduced to stupor by the wind [of age],

children.text: bhogairdhanena ca tadā vada kiṃ karoti
children.translated_text: tell me, what does one do then with pleasures and wealth?'
'Afflicted by disease, one does not even touch food with one's eyes;
in severe pain, the creature yearns for death.',
'When all medicines have failed and [the patient] cries out —

children.text: dhānyairdhanena ca tadā vada kiṃ karoti
children.translated_text: tell me, what does one do then with grain and wealth?'
'With kinsmen distressed by the interruption of sleep, abandoned by the anxious physician,
tormented by decoctions and poultices, shaken by attendants out of fear of drowsiness,
with hopes of recovery shattered, both feet grasped by the beloved —

children.text: paryante vapuṣaḥ karoti puruṣaḥ kiṃ śalyatulyairdhanaiḥ
children.translated_text: at the end of the body [i.e., at death], what does a man do with wealth that is like a thorn?'
'Adorned with ornaments worth crores of gold,
with precious jewels, elephants, horses, and vehicles —
[yet] one does not obtain life for even the blink of an eye
when seized by the forelock by Time at the appointed hour.'
'Unconscious, with a body like a piece of wood,
abandoned in an instant by sons, wife, and friends,
inheriting the good and bad of one's former deeds —
tell me, what does one do with jewels obtained through effort?'
'Therefore, do not be prideful, as if possessed by a spirit,
through the delusion born of abundant wealth.',
'These riches, familiar [only] with the dense darkness
of powerful greed, depart suddenly like flashes of lightning.'
'When the fortunes of wealth-lords have perished — in ancient times,
<s>Nala</s>, <s>Rāma</s>, and the sons of <s>Pāṇḍu</s> are heard to have entered the forest in distress.',
'<s>Śakra</s> (Indra), in separation from <s>Śrī</s> (Fortune), entered the hollow of a lotus stalk out of shame.',
'Who has stability when wealth is absent, [even] with various methods of safeguarding?'
Though admonished thus repeatedly by his wife,
he did not stir from his greed.
The innate nature of all beings —
by whom can it be restrained?
Then, in time, due to his greed,
deprived of physician and medicine,
clinging to his treasury and the pots of his hoards,
he perished.
Leaving behind ungiven and unenjoyed
wealth long guarded,
misers, like mice,
go to destruction upon their own destruction.
When he had gone to hell,
the king carried away his wealth.
In the end, the riches of the greedy
go to the king.
Then, for his son <s>Candana</s>,
even with the remaining wealth, which was still abundant,
there arose a great festival
of ample provisions, enjoyments, and expenditure.
'Let no one speak in the manner of <s>Nanda</s>,
that man of weak digestion,
saying "out of fear of the destruction of enjoyment"' —
thus the people declared every morning.
'Shame, shame on wealth — wretched death —
that is self-tormenting like <s>Nanda</s>'s!
Let everything be given, let everything be enjoyed!' —
thus said the townspeople.
Then, in time, a certain old blind woman,
a <s>caṇḍālī</s> (outcaste woman) named <s>Khaṇḍikā</s>,
living by the outer granary gate,
gave birth to a son.
Blind, hunchbacked, emaciated, lame,
leprous, with a swollen throat —
that son of hers was
like an assemblage of miseries.
When, due to [his] sins, the mother's milk
had dried up, he, helpless,
was raised out of compassion by the kinswomen
on the milk of a female dog.
This indeed is the strange working
of contradictory former deeds —
that the powerful, having nearly died in hardship,
survive, yet [then] fall into misfortune.
Covered with wounds oozing pus
and swarming with writhing worms,
corpse-like in appearance,
he lay upon a bed of damp grass.
Yet even toward him, out of extreme maternal love,
the mother maintained a firm attachment to her son.
The delusion of affection, latent in [past-life] impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>),
is indeed hard to overcome.
Growing up gradually,
grey with the ashes of the cremation ground,
he became a source of alarm
even to the fierce <s>piśācas</s> (flesh-eating spirits) of the burning-ground.
Walking supported by a staff,
repulsive with the oozing of leprosy,
He went by a path
by which no other traveled.
Meanwhile, at the <s>śrāddha</s> (memorial rite) day
of <s>Candana</s>'s father, a great
tumult arose from the distribution of food
to the throng of supplicants.
Then, taking a bowl,
that <s>caṇḍāla</s> (outcaste) child slowly,
a water-seeker, with difficulty
came to the ground before the door.
Seeing him, <s>Candana</s> from the mansion
[said:] 'This polluter of the <s>brāhmaṇas</s>' path —
let him be driven away! He has come [too] close!'
— thus he spoke with anger.
Frightened by the furrowing of the master's brow,
struck then with a staff
by the gatekeeper, that wretched boy
became like a [fallen] pigeon.
With the bone of his forehead split open,
drenched in flowing blood,
he fainted for a moment, then regained
his life — for the endurance of suffering.
The <s>caṇḍālī</s> (outcaste woman), nearby, hearing
his cry of pain,
approached and grieved, distressed,
touching his blood [and said:]
'By what merciless person was this
display of manliness shown?
Against one whose body is already sodden and wretched —
who has played the hero against him?'
'Seeing the unbearable condition of suffering
of this body composed entirely of sins —
at an occasion ripe for dispassion,
by whom was such cruelty committed?'
'Beholding this suffering of his,
this misery that melts the heart —
who could commit sin?
For sin is indeed the abode of calamities.'
'If he has not committed great sin
in a former birth,
then let it be told — has anyone seen
a condition as manifestly wretched as this?'
'Those who are seen afflicted
by the extreme pangs of diverse calamities —
they themselves are the teachers
in restraining men from the sowing of sin.'
'Of the brave toward those deserving compassion,
of enemies toward benefactors,
of deceivers toward the sinless —
who reckons such as sin?'
'Why do you cry aloud, my child?
Endure the pain born of the blow.
The workings of <s>karma</s> (action), which fashion misery,
strike at the vital points of embodied beings.'
While she was thus lamenting
and people had come to watch, the <s>Jina</s> (the Victor),
the friend of the friendless, an ocean
of compassion, came by that path,
consoling those exhausted by the toil
of clinging to the cycle of existence,
afflicted by faults of passion and the rest —
as if anointing the sky with the sandalwood of radiance,
seeing that one fallen into misfortune, broken
by terrible disease, sunken in calamity, distressed —
the blessed <s>Jinendra</s> (Lord of Victors), tender
with the <s>rasa</s> of compassion, paused for the alleviation of that suffering.
By his mere presence, for a moment
that one became free from pain, as if attaining well-being.
The sight of those whose intention is the welfare of beings
destroys sin and produces merit.
Then <s>Candana</s>, learning that the blessed
<s>Tathāgata</s> had arrived,
taking an offering of blossoming flowers,
went forth [to greet him].
The <s>Bhagavān</s> (Blessed One) too, by his wondrous
power, ascending a golden
lotus that had risen from the earth,
remained seated in the posture of crossed legs.
To [<s>Candana</s>], who was bowed down, clinging to his feet,
his hands busy with offerings, standing before him —
the <s>Bhagavān</s>, pleased, spoke
in the assembly of <s>bhikṣus</s> (monks), to <s>Candana</s>:
'Why was this wretch, though begging,
struck with anger?
Why was the mind not made
tender with compassion toward the pitiable one?'
'Those who are moist with compassion toward all beings
are of pure intention.',
'The cause of such sufferings
is a sullied mind.'
'Even toward those who have committed cruel offenses,
those harsh with enmity —
the good are not hard-hearted
toward those parched by the heat of afflictions.'
'This wretched one, tormented grievously
by miserliness in a former life,
through his unwillingness to give —
is now afflicted with bodily suffering.'
'This one was <s>Nanda</s>, your father [in a past life],
who, from his heap of stained wealth,
covered by the disease of sin,
has attained the state of a <s>caṇḍāla</s> (outcaste).'
'In yet another birth,
at the point of death from illness,
he gave some gold —
and thereby became wealthy [in this life].'
'That which one gives
at the point of death, in the final stage of suffering —
even that becomes unenjoyed by him
in other births, due to his miserliness.'
'Those by whom wealth was not given with compassion as its motive,
whose minds were set upon greed,
who danced to the tune of hoarding —
they lament the sinful conduct of their own lives.'
Having spoken thus, the <s>Bhagavān</s>
delivered a sacred <s>dharmadeśanā</s> (teaching of the Dharma),
by which <s>Candana</s> attained
<s>arhattva</s> (the state of an Arhat), worthy of the destruction of afflictions.
Therefore, let no man be prideful
as his wealth increases,
for wealth ruined by non-giving and non-enjoyment
is an ill omen for men both here and hereafter.
Third reflection:
If <s>vidyā</s> (learning), the sole cause of quelling the faults of <s>saṃsāra</s> (worldly existence),
produces the delusion of pride,
then it assuredly leads to darkness —
like the garland of rays of the sun in a clouded sky.
Even birds recite clearly
through the practice of training.
What is this pride in learning,
acquired with great difficulty and only in part?
That learning which destroys intoxication,
that prosperity which rains upon the needy,
that which follows <s>dharma</s> (righteousness) —
that is called true intelligence.
He who, though weighty with learning, becomes
lightweight through the collapse of good conduct —
to that learned fool,
that self-contradicting soul, salutations!
He who, having obtained learning,
has made his mind polluted with hostility —
that fool has, alas, covered himself
with heaps of dust after bathing.
Learning, like <s>Śrī</s> (Fortune), becomes despicable
through greed and through hatred;
it shines only through humility —
like a woman of good family, through modesty.
Learning, accompanied by contentment,
is desirable to the good, only so long as
it is not displayed for sale
in the marketplace of the king's court.
Good qualities remain pure only so long as
they are not examined by wicked ones
in the king's assembly — rinsed
and tested through argumentation.
Even a stone, which has no heart,
tests the essence of quality [in gold];
fitting indeed is the delight
of gold in falling into fire.
By poets, in the service of kings,
speech — charming with colorful ornaments —
has been made, through greed, a tool for others' use,
like a courtesan.
By debaters, speech — harsh from contact
with dispute-producing logic —
has been felled at the root of <s>dharma</s>,
like a saw-blade.
By logicians, made harsh solely
for the destruction of the brilliance of the good —
speech, wielded by cruel disputants,
is like the shears of a butcher.

children.text: śīlaṃ naiva bibharti kīrtivimale dhatte na dharme dhiyaṃ
children.translated_text: He bears no good conduct, sets no mind upon fame-brightening <s>dharma</s>,
through envy he extends the fault of harshness in speech toward the wise,
by logical argument he generally leads the work of the next world into doubt —
for that fool, skilled at the fruitless study of <s>śāstras</s>, what use is learning?
Those who are quarrelsome in assemblies, tormented like a thorn by others' fame,
who, through self-praise, earnestly cover the qualities of the truly accomplished —
for those with anger-bitter, glaring eyes, breathing the hot air of hatred,
learning, like the blazing jewel-crest of black-hooded serpents, is a source of public alarm.
Through bad conduct, [learning] comes to be pitied;
through hostility, it becomes impure.
Learning, struck by the curse of pride,
perishes together with [one's] lifespan.
In a hermitage, two great sages,
honored among the wise —
<s>Raibhya</s> and <s>Bharadvāja</s> — friends of old,
established their abode.
<s>Raibhya</s> had two sons,
mirrors of spotless learning,
admirable to the knowers of virtues —
<s>Sarvāvasu</s> and <s>Parāvasu</s>.
<s>Bharadvāja</s>'s son was
named <s>Yavakrīta</s>; sons
generally remain unlearned
when pampered by a father's affection.
That youth, seeing <s>Raibhya</s>'s sons
famous everywhere for their scriptural learning,
[and comparing them] to himself, became envious
and filled with remorse.
He went to the bank of the <s>Jāhnavī</s> (<s>Gaṅgā</s>)
and, emaciated from long fasting,
with body motionless, performed
intense austerity for the attainment of learning.
<s>Śatakratu</s> (<s>Indra</s>) himself came to him,
whose soul was scorched by austerity,
and said: 'What is this vain obstinacy
of yours, O little son of a sage?'
'How can learning be attained
without studying from a teacher's mouth?
Scholarship without practice —
[that is like] a crown of sky-flowers!'
'What use is learning to you now?
Your childhood, fit for learning, has passed.',
'Apply yourself to that
which is truly the fruit of learning.'
'Good conduct, devotion to others' welfare,
absence of arrogance, patience, fortitude,
and freedom from greed — these are
the brilliant fruits of learning's ripening.'
'Learning bereft of discrimination,
dried up by the heat of hatred and anger,
struck by the thunderbolt of pride —
is fruitless, like a blasted creeper.'
'One corrupted by hostility directs his intellect
toward scripture for this purpose:',
'By debates I shall bring about
the humiliation of the wise.'
'Having abandoned tranquility and contentment —
the primary fruit of learning —
by various perverse paths
go those who seek the fruit of wealth.'
'That [learning] which serves not the benefit of men,
neither others' nor one's own —
what use is that burdensome learning,
[merely] a collection of leaves?'
'That by which injustice is, through bold argument,
led to appear as justice,
and justice, through greed, as injustice —
what use is that base learning?'
'That which, through constant self-praise,
is displayed in the assembly — like a wife
with garments thrown open —
what use is that shameless learning?'
'That which, devoid of practice,
merely through recitation alone
entertains the people —
what use is that parrot-learning?'
'That which is concealed before the learned
and displayed before the ignorant,
and not given to disciples —
what use is that deceitful learning?'
'That which, concealing others' excellence,
is displayed for sale
again and again before the wealthy —
what use is that merchandise-learning?'
'That by which the terrible ocean of <s>saṃsāra</s>,
infested with <s>makaras</s> (sea-monsters), is not crossed —
that which constantly binds the mind —
what use is that delusion-learning?'
'That by which life is consumed
through the effort of constant practice,
with obstruction of the three aims of life —
what use is that toilsome learning?'
'That which produces in men neither
an intellect fit for discrimination
nor a mind imbued with dispassion —
what use is that inert learning?'
'That by which, through disputes over purity and impurity,
the status of a learned <s>brāhmaṇa</s> is abandoned,
that which is yoked to false pride —
what use is that hypocritical learning?'
'That by which the torment
of envy's thorn toward others arises,
which robs one of peaceful sleep —
what use is that thorn-learning?'
'That whose excellence is proclaimed
by stealing others' sayings
and calling them one's own —
what use is that thief-learning?'
'That whose enthusiasm is destroyed by lack of practice,
which is defeated by another,
which generates embarrassment through dullness —
what use is that feeble learning?'
'That by which the greed of the exceedingly wealthy
and the passion of the renunciant
are not pacified —
what use is that false learning?'
'That by which, having taken refuge with a king,
one who denigrates others' merits
destroys the elevation of generosity and honor —
what use is that fault-learning?'
'That which, though at its peak at home,
does not function in the assembly,
due to the seizure of the failure of wit —
what use is that mute learning?'
'That by which, like dogs
who are fierce, malicious seekers of scraps,
quarrels arise —
what use is that slaughter-learning?'
'That which is forgotten by the conceited one,
[merely] going back and forth in the throat,
diminished like a [dying] creature's breath —
what use is that dead learning?'
'That by which the alchemist grows old,
the physician is chronically ill,
and the metallurgist is poor —
what use is that laughable learning?'
'That by which innocent deer
are tormented by traps and keen arrows —
which depends on the noose of desire —
what use is that hunter's learning?'
'That by which harm to others is wrought
through charms of subjugation and the like —
which follows <s>yantras</s> (mechanical devices) and <s>tantras</s> (rituals) —
what use is that fraudulent learning?'
'That by which the teacher [falls] through arrogance, the poet through envy,
the ascetic through attachment to enjoyments,
the king through sin, the <s>brāhmaṇa</s> through anger —
that learning is obstructed.'
'Those qualities of learning in the wise
which serve as the foundation of discrimination —
[only those are true]; the rest, equal to petty crafts,
are merely means of livelihood.'
'Like a <s>vīṇā</s> for the deaf,
like a flirtatious woman for the blind,
like a garland of flowers for one without a nose —
learning is fruitless for the obstinate.'
'When learning is destroyed by hatred and pride,
intelligence by desire and anger,
and livelihood by greed and delusion —
of what use is their lifespan?'
'Keep difficult grammar far away — it is disturbed by the wasting of <s>dhātus</s> (verbal roots / bodily constituents);

children.text: mīmāṃsā virasā na śoṣayati kiṃ tarkairalaṃ karkaśaiḥ
children.translated_text: <s>Mīmāṃsā</s> is tasteless — does it not parch? Enough of harsh logic!

children.text: na kṣībaḥ patati smarabhramakaraiḥ kiṃ navyakāvyāsavais
children.translated_text: Does not the drunkard fall through the intoxicating new wine of poetry, which produces the vertigo of love?
Therefore, for the eternal welfare of those of tranquil minds, dispassion (<s>vairāgya</s>) is the [true] medicine of health.'
Thus addressed by the king of the gods,
he did not waver from his resolve.
For those seized by [false] pride,
the evil possession is hard to remove.
Then, having become an old <s>brāhmaṇa</s>,
<s>Śakra</s> (<s>Indra</s>), with handfuls of sand, slowly
proceeded to build
a bridge over the <s>Gaṅgā</s>.
Seeing him, fixed in
fruitless toil and vain enterprise,
the sage's son, filled with pity,
approached and asked with a smile:
'O <s>brāhmaṇa</s>, what is this obstinacy
of yours in this futile endeavor?
A fruitless [yet] laborious task —
the wise do not perform.
In this [river] of crooked waves,
in the water agitated like a swing —
how could a bridge, a cause for laughter,
be made with handfuls of sand?
When the sage's son had spoken thus,
the <s>brāhmaṇa</s> addressed him:
Ah, in advising others,
everyone is a learned man!
You wish to attain by force, through austerity,
knowledge that has not been studied —
just as your effort is fruitless,
so am I another dullard.
Having heard these words of the <s>brāhmaṇa</s>,
truthful [and thus] struck speechless for a reply,
yet still firm in his resolve,
he did not waver from his task.
Then, by his intense austerity,
<s>Śakra</s> (<s>Indra</s>) granted him the best of boons,
by which he became a treasury of all knowledge
in an instant.
Having acquired knowledge, he, full of enthusiasm,
quickly went to his own hermitage
and reported to his father the story
of having attained the fruit of his austerity.
Him — intoxicated with pride, unwearied,
speaking in polished and refined [language] —
<s>Bharadvāja</s>, even in his delight,
addressed as if troubled by perspiration:
Son, you have acquired knowledge;
why speak of the pain of austerity?
But from fear of what is to come,
this does not seem proper to me.
Near here is the <s>tapovana</s> (ascetic grove)
of the irascible <s>Raibhya</s>;
his two sons, blinded by the pride of learning,
[are] <s>Arvāvasu</s> and <s>Parāvasu</s>.
Those two, mad with unrelenting learning,
and you, a freshly-minted scholar —
in the meeting of [such people], strife,
full of hatred, is always close at hand.
Bearing a stiff neck, suffering headaches at the mere mention of another's superiority,
his composure overwhelmed by agitated wandering, raving, and great agitation,
breathing hot sighs of terrible anger from the entry of the poison of inner hatred —
dreadful is the derangement of the newly-learned, a breeding ground for a fearful fever.
When you go there,
disputing what is proper and improper,
from the curse of the sage
there will inevitably be a crushing of [your] pride.
Through perceptions like the knowledge of silver in a shell,
or seeing blue as yellow —
the demoness of the pride of learning
produces madness indeed.
This destruction through the teaching of knowledge
has been sought by you;
<s>Raibhya</s>'s hermitage should not be visited —
do this if you heed my words.
Though told this repeatedly by his father,
he went to the sons of <s>Raibhya</s>
and through the weariness of disputes
always displayed the intoxication of the pride of learning.
Him, drunk with arrogance,
those two, with angry, fearsome, frowning, wrathful faces,
addressed — they whose minds were pierced
by the trident of hatred for [another's] learning:
Since you are younger than us both
in age and in learning,
[yet] you make insults through your disputations —
therefore, may your life be destroyed!
Though thus addressed by them in anger,
he did not desist from his arrogance;
neither the pleased nor the angered
do those puffed up with pride regard.
Meanwhile, [a season] with the playful coquetry
of the frowning brows of garlands of wandering bees,
the flower-season — the time
of women whose lovers are away — arrived.
Scattering petals, with eyes made turbid
by the pollen of flowers,
the <s>Malaya</s> breezes moved about
as if they were envious scholars.
Through the playful, sweet, and graceful
display of [their] voices, again and again,
a rivalry arose among the <s>kokilas</s> (cuckoos)
as among poets.
When <s>Raibhya</s> had gone with his two sons
to the river bank to bathe,
the son of <s>Bharadvāja</s>, having come,
entered his hermitage.
There, busy with the gathering of flowers,
[he saw] the lawful wife of <s>Purāvasu</s> —
named <s>Suprabhā</s>,
[whose beauty] put to shame the pride of <s>Rati</s>'s form.
With members [that made] the gazelles
lingering in the hermitage yard
take a lesson in coquetry
from her playful, sidelong glances.
Seeing her, moon-faced,
a deity of the bliss of love,
the son of the sage instantly
transgressed all bounds.
He, a celibate student, made restless
by new desire,
though inexperienced in speaking words befitting desire,
nevertheless addressed her:
This maddening form of yours,
befitting the Mind-born [<s>Kāma</s>],
makes my mind
as if overflowing with attachment.
Abandoning the discipline of learning,
casting off the restraints of the guru,
my mind has turned toward you —
bound by the love of a former birth.
I know that the fruit of this deed
will ripen in its consequence;
yet I am unable to restrain my desire —
what can I do?
Not by learning, not by wealth,
not by conduct, not by action,
can the mind be restrained
when it has set forth on the path of love.
Having spoken thus, as she — with eyes
bewildered with fear — turned toward the hermitage
and began to go, he, approaching,
seized the edge of her garment.
Like a plantain [dragged] by an elephant,
forcibly [dragged] by him in that solitary place,
being pulled, she addressed him,
her fingers trembling as she gestured 'no':
Do not, do not sully the pure
character of mine and of yourself;
is this the fitting fruit
of blameless learning?
Abandoning modesty — like your own bride
in the white garment of good character —
you seize with your hand the hem of the garment
of another man's wife!
'What is this improper [act]!' — seeing this,
surely the water-pot,
with raised neck, as if in curiosity,
gazes at your face.
Bearing within a new delight
in the arrows of <s>Kāma</s>,
your burden of matted hair and bark-garments,
like a tree's, is not for the sake of peace.
Through the mere evil intention,
downcast with shame,
your rosary has fallen
as if in fear of your touch, with trembling beads.
On the lotus-seat of <s>Sarasvatī</s>,
on your lip-covering that trembles with prayer —
this speech of wicked counsel is unfitting
in the mouth of you, a wise man.
This ground of the ascetic grove,
which gives rise to discernment — how
does it give rise to desire in you,
as if [it were] a mother for one who has not conquered himself?
The untamable burden of youth,
like a runaway horse,
in every way throws the slack-spirited one
into a pit in an instant.
Shame on the intellect! What use is discernment?
Let learning rest far away!
— for those by whom the mind, faltering
in the distortions of worldly existence, is not held firm.
Where is learning — whose understanding deliberates
upon what should and should not be done?
And where is this delusion, partner
of the great sin of wicked deeds?
Though thus addressed, when he
did not relinquish his unyielding grip,
she, terrified of the theft of [her] virtue,
then reflected:
What shall I do, caught in a deserted place,
helpless, by this reckless [man]?
Those who have abandoned the restraints of dharma —
what will they not do, when unobstructed?
This one, tormented by desire,
will not be turned back by words;
those inflamed by lust, anger, and pride
are [only] deceived by soothing speech.
Having reflected thus, she
addressed him softly, with gentle words:
Go — I myself will come
at night to the empty vine-bower.
At this time, my father-in-law,
having bathed with his sons, has not returned;
before him, who is like blazing fire —
what will you do?
Thus told by her, he departed,
believing her words to be true;
even the hard-to-obtain, those deluded by desire
consider easy.
Then, when <s>Raibhya</s> returned
and stood before the fire-house,
his daughter-in-law addressed him, weeping
as if with the smoke of the fire of anger:
Father, the wicked son of <s>Bharadvāja</s>,
your friend's son,
today, in this solitary place, has gone so far as to
solicit me for the violation of my virtue.
He, seized by an unyielding obsession,
was deceived by me [saying] 'I will come';
I could not otherwise free myself
from his hands while remaining unharmed.
Hearing this, the sage instantly,
blazing with wrath,
became like the sun
cruel with the fall of an ill-omened meteor.
Discernment shines within
those of calm minds who possess learning;
at the time of disturbance, delusion [rules] the mind,
and learning [stays] in the book.
Then, sighing, with eyes reddened
by the onset of the fever of wrath,
with trembling lower lip as if [chanting]
an incantation of sorcery, he declared:
Alas! <s>Bharadvāja</s>
labored over his son's education
and taught him dharma with great effort —
[only] to strip another's wife!
Having said this, unable from the agitation
of indignation to say more,
he entered the fire-house
and set about [his] retaliatory [rite].
Tearing out, with terrible, swelling fury,
a matted lock, tawny as a full-grown fire,
he offered it into the flames
like the mane of cruel wrath.
When the second [lock] was offered,
a fearsome <s>rākṣasa</s> (demon) bearing a trident,
accompanied by a <s>kṛtyā</s> (female fiend), arose
and, bowing, addressed the sage:
What shall I do, O sage? For whose
destruction have I been created?
I am ready, at your command,
to burn even the three worlds.
Thus speaking, <s>Raibhya</s> addressed him,
cruel of form:
Go to the son of <s>Bharadvāja</s> —
devour the [so-called] scholar!
Thus commanded by him,
that [demon], going forth, shaking the earth,
seeing the sage's son in the midst
of his ablutions, rushed at him from afar.
When that night-roamer rushed at him swiftly
with blazing trident,
the sage's son, his movement broken by fear,
found no refuge.
Fleeing, he reached swiftly
his father's hermitage,
and entering the fire-house was blocked
by a <s>śūdra</s>, [thus] polluted by impure touch.
Touched by the servant, deprived of purity,
he fell to the ground in his confusion;
then, struck by the trident of the <s>rākṣasa</s>,
he was instantly reduced to ashes.
Meanwhile, <s>Bharadvāja</s>,
entering his own hermitage
and seeing its shade destroyed,
thought anxiously:
The fires that always rise before me
as I return from gathering flowers and fruits —
why do they today appear
as if motionless?
Having reflected thus, the sage saw before him
his son [reduced to] ashes out of fear;
and hearing the account told by the servant,
he fell to the ground.
Regaining consciousness slowly,
he spoke, choked with tears:
May <s>Raibhya</s> too, though learned, in time
meet death through his own son.
Alas, son! Even though protected,
[you are] subject to the fall of momentary destruction;
I cannot live without you,
with this body full of faults.
Having spoken thus, the sage entered
the funeral fire from grief for his son;
even among the great, sorrows born of fresh pride
have an unbroken course.
Then, when time had passed slowly,
to the house of king <s>Bṛhadyumna</s>
<s>Arvāvasu</s> and <s>Parāvasu</s>
went as sacrificial priests.
When the long sacrificial session
of that king of great splendor
was properly commenced, a certain rising
of pride from gifts and honors occurred in those two priests.
Once, at dusk at the end of a day,
<s>Parāvasu</s>, returning
to his own hermitage,
saw his father before him,
[clad] in a black deerskin upper garment —
and mistaking him for a deer,
struck him with his staff, compelled by [<s>Bharadvāja</s>'s] curse;
by that [blow], he (<s>Raibhya</s>) became senseless.
Seeing his father slain,
distraught with fear of <s>brahmahatyā</s> (the sin of killing a <s>brāhmaṇa</s>),
he went to the sacrificial ground
and reported the matter to his brother.
<s>Arvāvasu</s> addressed him:
Brother, what can be done against fate?
From whose will arise
reversals of such a kind.
He who seeks dharma obtains sin;
he who seeks virtue, the ruin of virtue;
when fate turns hostile,
he who seeks wealth [obtains] poverty.
I will undertake the severe expiation
for <s>brahmahatyā</s> on your behalf;
you complete for this lord of the earth
the full performance of the sacrifice.
Having spoken thus, <s>Arvāvasu</s>,
undertaking the vow for his brother's purification from sin,
performed severe expiatory rites
at all the holy places.
When he, having completed his vow, arrived
at the sacrificial ground of the king,
<s>Parāvasu</s>, the father-slayer, recognizing him
from afar, reflected:
This one has come at the time of fees,
to seize my share;
by my ill fortune, even though long tormented
by severe vows, he still lives.
Having reflected thus, he approached
and addressed the king,
having fallen into the lap of greed and jealousy,
desiring sin:
O king, this one, defiled by the sin
of <s>brahmahatyā</s> (killing a <s>brāhmaṇa</s>),
is entering your sacrificial ground without hesitation —
my brother — let him be stopped!
Thus told by him, the ungrateful one,
the king, through a reversal [of truth],
out of ignorance prohibited the entry
of that sinless one.
Like the blind, [kings] do not see
what is fit and unfit, beneficial and harmful;
they go by the very path
by which they are led.
By the gift of false accusation against his brother,
he (<s>Arvāvasu</s>) was not angered;
the wise consider fate
the cause of mistreatment.
By that compassion of his,
by that state of being unperturbed,
the gods seated at the sacrifice were pleased
and addressed him:
By this tranquility of yours,
we are pleased with you, O sage;
though worthy of a boon, O one of excellent conduct,
let the choicest boon be taken.
Thus addressed by the gods with affection,
he spoke to them with joined palms:
If I am worthy of your boon,
let what I desire be granted.
The son of <s>Bharadvāja</s>, who was slain
by sorcery at my father's [command] —
let him live, and also his father,
their memory of the cruel mistreatment erased.
Our father, who was killed by <s>Parāvasu</s>
in the delusion of [mistaking him for] a deer —
May he too, his anger forgotten,
in peace, attain life.
When this boon was thus requested by him,
'So be it!' was declared by those gods.
Yavakrita, Bharadvaja,
and the Raibhyas regained their lives.

children.text: ityete munayo 'pi darpaviphale yāte śrute śocyatāṃ
children.translated_text: Thus even these sages, when their vain pride came to naught, fell into a pitiable state;
blinded again by anger, with the clear light of discernment destroyed,

children.text: śīle rāgamahoṣmaṇā vigalite dveṣeṇa nāśaṃ gatāḥ
children.translated_text: with character melted away by the great heat of passion -- they perished through hatred.
Whose learning, tainted by the impurity of the pride of wealth, bestows virtue upon another?
For the tranquility of the mind, by one who has abandoned hatred and pride,
effort must be made in every way by the wise;
the lamp of learning, for those whose eyes are agitated by desire and anger,
is but a fruitless light for those blinded by pride.
Non-covetousness is the supreme wealth,
non-violence is the supreme austerity,
freedom from deceit is the supreme learning,
blameless, for the wise.
The learning of <s>Shukra</s>, [used] to steal the wealth of <s>Dhana</s> (Kubera),
augmented by the deception of noble pretenses, is pitiable;
and the learning of <s>Kaca</s>, though born from <s>Vacaspati</s> (<s>Brihaspati</s>) himself,
was rendered fruitless through deceit.

children.text: spṛśati matiṃ nahi teṣāṃ dveṣaviṣaḥ kalisarpaḥ /
children.translated_text: The <s>Kali</s>-serpent of hatred, whose venom is envy, does not touch the minds of those

children.text: yadi śamavimalamatīnāṃ svamanasi bhavati na darpaḥ //
children.translated_text: whose intellects are purified by tranquility -- if there is no pride in their own minds.
Fourth investigation.
Of men whose beauty lasts but a day, comparable to lotuses,
what is this pride in their transient form?
Their radiance of form is but momentary,
like the color of garments dyed with turmeric.
The body of a child, by nature like a painting
devoid of outline, limb-division, and detail,
blossoms only through youth,
as the <s>shirisha</s> flower blossoms through the festival of <s>Caitra</s> (spring).
The face of the young, hairless, with the beauty of the full moon,
remains so for but a few days;
then, when the wide net of the beard has appeared,
it bears the likeness of a lotus entangled in moss.
A painting by smoke, a lotus by frost,
the moon's orb by the dark fortnight,
cool water by summer's heat -- they do not shine,
nor does beautiful form with the descent of old age.
Old age, whose defects of desire are fashioned by
the devouring of flesh and blood seized in an instant as form --
seizing people by the hair,
like a courtesan, devours their wealth.
Time, the worker of wondrous deeds, imperceptible to embodied beings,
by the gradual process of ripening, moment by moment,
through the power of transformation,
makes the beautiful ugly -- a swift, cunning current.
The course of time with its speed is not perceived --
this time that produces the confusion of a spinning wheel.
He who yesterday was a child is today in manifest youth;
by morning, body worn by old age -- the very same one.
In the three-part division of people's three stages of life,
youth alone bestows form -- nothing else;
and when that youth is afflicted by the defects of intoxication, madness, disease, bodily injury,
and visible marks -- where then is beauty?
When a man, burned by sorrow, grieves,
having abandoned food, his face pallid with grief,
neither bathing nor rising nor even sleeping --

children.text: tadā kva rūpaṃ kva ca yauvanaśrīḥ
children.translated_text: then where is beauty? And where is the glory of youth?
When one stands like a corpse, reduced to mere bones,
in a prison, with dusty, upstanding hair,
body blackened by scattered lice and impurities --
then where has the pride of beauty gone?
When, constantly embracing the suffering of servility,
the body is ruined by the wandering of service,
with knees broken from the perpetual fatigue of travel --
then one endowed with beauty has no beauty.
When, struck by blows, all limbs are shattered,
with lips and nose broken, eyes and teeth split open --
a young man assumes a form as if of a <s>pishaca</s> (goblin) --
then too, beauty has lost its true nature.
When a man is neither wise nor a chastiser of enemies,
nor eloquent, but equal to a painted figure --
then, better an ugly person of admirable character
than a handsome one who is pleasing only through thoughtless beauty.
When a man, poor and without garments,
hides in shame and grimaces excessively,
with wrinkles forming on his cheeks --
then even a handsome man is utterly ugly.
In an assembly of scholars, amid debaters and foremost poets, a fool
ignorant of language, who is laughed at by name with words of praise for <s>Shankara</s>'s vehicle [the bull],
sold in the marketplace of a foreign land, like a mute person among cheats --
of what use is the beauty of form to a man with the lovely body of an ornamental peacock?
Seeing time drinking life with the finger-circle of moments,
with the cupped hands of days and nights,
seeing form and body -- for whom
do the limbs not become languid with the awareness of dissolution?
Beauty, youth, valor, the pleasures of love,
the power of wisdom, wealth, and body --
the bee of time devours completely from all sides,
as it devours the filaments of lotuses.
Once, in the company of <s>Gandharvas</s>,
in the assembly hall, to the lord of <s>Shaci</s> (<s>Indra</s>),
all the <s>Apsarases</s> rendered service
with dance and with song.
Among them shone the beautiful one,
like <s>Kaishiki</s> among the dramatic styles --
<s>Urvashi</s>, as if proclaiming
the friendship of the moon and the lotus in her own face.
The gods who had come there to attend upon <s>Shakra</s> (<s>Indra</s>),
seeing her, the moon-faced one,
considered themselves blessed,
having attained the state of being limbs of <s>Shringara</s> (the erotic sentiment).
Dancing, she shone, reflected
in the central gems of the necklace,
as if simultaneously entering
the hearts of the celestials.
The swans, vanquished by her gait, hid themselves
in the celestial chariots of the gods;
the deer in the moon, conquered by her sidelong glance,
closed its eyes for a moment.
Upon her breasts, the fallen garland
of blue lotus petals, slipped from her crest,
appeared like a garland of envious <s>Apsaras</s> eyes
fallen upon her bosom.
The burden of pearls released from the broken string within the necklace,
which had been disrupted by the whirling bee-like spinning of her enthusiastic coquetry,
clinging to the expanse of her breasts, in the form of drops of nectar cascading from her moon-face,
created for a moment the splendor of water-drops from the dense perspiration produced by the exertion of the delight of her dance.
Seeing <s>Manmatha</s> (the god of love) become thrilled with horripilation while watching her dance,
<s>Rati</s> (his consort) made a curtain before him with the dust of her beautiful form, gathered by her sighs;
seeing even <s>Hari</s>'s (<s>Vishnu</s>'s) succession of glances fixed there, <s>Shaci</s> (<s>Indra</s>'s wife) grew faint,
and with the bees of her playful lotus agitated by anger, she produced darkness by closing her eyes.

children.text: vighnaṃ na cakrurnanu nṛttalīlāsaṃdarśane puṇyavatāṃ narāṇām /
children.translated_text: They caused no obstruction -- for the blessed among men, in watching the play of her dance,
the eyes of those captivated by <s>Urvashi</s>'s beauty were devoid of blinking.
Of the two <s>Ashvins</s>, the gods who were there,
foremost bearers of the sweetness of beauty,
a conversation arose between them,
their minds attracted by her qualities.
One said: 'Ah! The beauty
of this trembling-eyed one!
Even sages, whose vow is the closing of their eyes,
are thrown into agitation by it.'
'In this assembly, into whose face
do these glances fall, glances of noble birth,
bashfully curved with the discourse
of <s>Smara</s>'s (Love's) amorous dialogue?'
'In the mutual gazing
of two who have met,
<s>Ananga</s> (the Bodiless One) has secretly deposited
the entire treasure of <s>Shringara</s> (the erotic sentiment).'
'Upon the neck of one who has cast off his body in battle,
eagerly, the arm-embrace --
upon whom will this trembling-eyed one,
having descended from the stage, bestow it?'
While he was speaking thus, the other one
addressed him with a smile:
'Ah! Have you forgotten
the moon on earth -- <s>Pururravas</s>?'
'The ornament of valor in all directions,
the beauty-mark of the earth,
resplendent through the enjoyment of <s>Urvashi</s> --
whose fame is thus celebrated.'
'By him, through beauty, qualities, and valor,
this <s>Urvashi</s> has been captivated;
even while standing before <s>Shakra</s> (<s>Indra</s>),
she dwells with him in mind.'
'On account of the similarity of his beauty,
even he who was born in the lineage of the cool-rayed (moon) feels ashamed;
<s>Smara</s> (the god of love), envious,
does not tell his story before <s>Rati</s> (his consort).'
'I do not know -- alas! What is this
grudge of the flower-bowed one (<s>Kama</s>),
that he does not even place in his hand
the five arrows that are rightly his?'
'The husband of the entire ocean-girdled earth,
whose arms hang down to his knees --
bearing him, weighty even as a plaything, in her heart,
how the slender one dances -- we do not understand!'
'That king must be seen,
even without occasion, with effort;
who knows how long such a gem
remains, earned by merit?'
Having spoken thus, the two, having resolved
to behold the lord of the earth,
when the dance was over, bowed to the enemy of <s>Jambha</s> (<s>Indra</s>)
and departed for the earth.
Arriving at the capital
of <s>Pururravas</s>, in a moment
the two entered unhindered,
ushered by the doorkeepers out of respect for gods.
The two beheld him in the midst of his bath,
his body being anointed with oil,
like the moon with the fresh butter of nectar,
to which affection clings.
His body, having bathed, with bracelets and
precious jeweled bangles removed,
shone, its ornament being loveliness itself,
with elevated splendor.
Of him, with his ear-loops and chains empty,
the throat attained
a special charm
even in the unadorned setting.
Having considered the decorum
of that beauty's nobility, the two <s>Ashvins</s>
praised the wondrous
surpassing excellence of the Creator's workmanship.
He, with palms joined in joy,
having seated the two,
with a clear heart, asked them
the reason for their coming.
The two said: 'O lord of the earth,
O Cupid of the world!
The beauty that is the ornament of the three worlds --
yours -- we have come to behold.'
'By nature, in the creation of the world,
with unbounded appreciation of virtues,
as if your beauty were the very essence of the curiosity to behold --
we see in you the creation of <s>Prajapati</s>.'
'You have been beheld -- the earth,
the moon in its full orb --
from drinking the nectar of your beauty,
the delight obtained -- what more can be said?'
Thus addressed by them with affection, the king, with a slightly blossoming smile,
spoke to the two, an honor surpassing what was due to one being honored:
'Through your visit,
I have become a recipient of grace;
the worthy come to see
those who are to be seen -- solely by the merit of their merit.'
'Pilgrimage, the company of the virtuous,
the great festival of worshipping the worshipful --
in this tasteless, essenceless
samsara (worldly existence), these are the collection of essence.'
'By me, still anointed for my bath,
the proper respect has not been shown to you both --
the reverence of worship for auspiciousness,
free from the thorn of unfulfilled merit.'
'Please remain for a moment
in the fire-chamber;
having completed my bath, I shall come
to fulfill the claim of hospitality and worship.'
Thus addressed by him, the two went
to the fire-temple,
thinking: 'We shall see the king when bathed and adorned' -- out of curiosity.
Then the king, having completed his bath,
adorned with all ornaments,
accompanied by the chief priest,
approached their vicinity.
The two, seeing the protector of the earth
with his star-like necklace and crown,
said nothing for a moment,
despondent, with downcast faces.
When the king had worshipped them,
the chief priest asked the two:
'Why, suddenly,
does there appear displeasure in you both?'
'Has any transgression of courtesy on our part
become, perchance, a cause of your displeasure?'
Asked thus by the chief priest,
the two gently spoke to him:
'There is no displeasure in us,
nor any transgression on your part;
rather, it is the astonishment at beholding
all things being swallowed by time.'
'Just now this king
was seen, even during his anointing, as he was;
by the momentary ripening of time,
he is no longer seen as that same one.'
'In the forest of fuel that is each day,
constantly burned by the fire of the sun,
the colorful painting of beauty is brought
by the smoke of time to colorlessness.'
'Having ascertained this constant impermanence
of all things --
who would take pride in beauty,
which is like a painting on the canvas of a dream?'
'Seeing forms worn out by old age,
bodies afflicted by disease,
lifespans licked away by time --
who could be intoxicated with pride?'
'This world that is beheld,
with its vast appearances and transformations --
these are but swollen
drops of semen.'
'Ah, this subtle, imperceptible
step-by-step progression of time!
Through the transformation of its ripening,
everything assumes another form.'
'That wave of loveliness of the king's body
which existed at the moment of his bath --
it was drunk up in an instant by time,
which had begun something suited to another moment.'
'The measure of one's full life-span,
of beauty, and of wealth,
flows away ceaselessly for men,
like the stream of a water-clock's march.'
'Of the kalas, kashthas, and muhurtas
of time, passing with speed --
the movement cannot be perceived in its divisions,
like the flickering of a lamp's flames.'
'A child at dawn, a youth at midday,
an elder at sunset --
day after day, even the sun itself
is made so by the play of time.'
'The oceans dry up, embracing the directions with their dense waves;
the mountain-lords, towering with lofty peaked crowns, go to destruction;
even the earth perishes, together with the elephants of the directions -- by whose power,

children.text: sarvāśī satataṃ pradhāvati mahākālaḥ sa ko 'pyākulaḥ
children.translated_text: great <s>Kala</s> (Time), the all-devourer, rushes constantly -- restless, unidentifiable.'
Having spoken thus and taken leave of the king,
the two <s>Ashvins</s> departed for heaven;
and the king, through contemplating their words,
became one whose pride in beauty had been pacified.
Therefore, the wise one, having reflected, should not cultivate
the pride of wondrous beauty and its display;
in this dense proliferation of the delusion of <s>samsara</s>,
beauty is but the flash of a lightning-creeper.
In the morning, a tender bud, then gradually with its budding like a woman's breast in beauty,
with the lovely radiance of a playful smile blooming, then a full-blown blossom,
afterward withered in body, loose and trembling, the lotus, scattered by the winds,
on that very same day dries up on the muddy, soaked bank.
Congenital deformity; <s>Yayāti</s>, whose beauty was stolen by old age, went [to old age] long ago;
<s>Nala</s>, whose fame had challenged <s>Kāma</s>'s (Love's) through his splendor, became hideous in form;
the captivating body of <s>Saudāsa</s> became a source of terror to living beings —
who can maintain steadfastness regarding beauty, which fades daily, being impermanent?

Therefore, having reflected that beauty is unstable, and upon the true nature of existence, the wise should undertake the pacification of the passions born of beauty, for the attainment of a firm state. //
Fifth Inquiry
'I am a hero, skilled in smashing the ranks of fierce adversaries,
mighty, the lord of troops of horses and elephants in the army' —
thus the pride that swells within men whose arm-strength has conquered the world
becomes, when dissolved by time, an object of contempt.
What is this pride in valor for a man?
The quality of heroism is observed even among animals.
That which lacks propriety, is devoid of discipline,
and is impoverished of compassion — that, they do not call valor.
The valor of a child, who is delicate as a flower,
[lies] in striking his mother during affectionate smiles;
the valor of an old man, whose limbs' joints are loosened,
[lies] in self-praise on the paths of former tales.
The valor of a young man in the middle third of life,
which is itself overwhelmed by the effects of pride —
that, due to the manifold nature of mental disposition,
undergoes extreme reversal by turns.
Of the mind, which is by nature as restless as the wind,
what [stability] can be achieved, given its manifold qualities?
He by whom the enemy's army was routed yesterday —
that very same one today becomes timid and unsteady;
<s>Śakra</s> (<s>Indra</s>) was swallowed by <s>Vṛtra</s> in battle,
and that same <s>Śakra</s> slew <s>Vṛtra</s> with a thunderbolt of foam.
fickle with pride, she does not embrace one alone —
royal fortune (<s>rājalakṣmī</s>) is [indeed] like a drunken courtesan.

children.text: yaḥ kārtavīryasya ca doḥsahasraṃ viccheda vīro nahi yudhi jāmadagnyaḥ /
children.translated_text: He who heroically severed the thousand arms of <s>Kārtavīrya</s> in battle — <s>Jāmadagnya</s> (<s>Paraśurāma</s>) — he, when <s>Rāma</s>'s hand had grasped the arrow, became a supplicant through the pitiableness of his Brahmin status.

<s>Rāma</s> too, out of greed for obtaining the skill of an ally, performed the pitiful service of taking refuge in a monkey. The glory of a hero's valor, like the winter season, withers and attenuates when licked by time.
<s>Vālin</s>, the monkey, having seized with one hand
ten-headed <s>Rāvaṇa</s> — who was as powerful as <s>Kailāsa</s> shaking with its exuberance —
placed him in the knot of his armpit-hem
and proceeded to perform the twilight rites at the seven oceans.
Kings famed for their ferocity in battle
were formerly bound by King <s>Jarāsaṃdha</s>;
he was split in two by <s>Bhīmasena</s>,
whose arms were his weapons, by tearing apart [his] joints.
<s>Bhīma</s> too had his courage shattered by <s>Karṇa</s>,
his power bewildered, and was released by [Karṇa's] mercy;
while <s>Karṇa</s>, before <s>Arjuna</s> whose bow was fully drawn,
came moment by moment to the status of a supplicant.
<s>Arjuna</s>, having abandoned the womenfolk of <s>Kṛṣṇa</s>,
departed, overcome by the force of cowherds;
the course of valor — following the path of fate —
is unknowable, fickle as an elephant's ear.
A coward comes to possess heroism,
and a hero too comes to cowardice;
there is no fixed stability
of this fickle valor anywhere.
<s>Bāṇa</s>, [though protected] by the three-eyed one (<s>Śiva</s>), the foe of <s>Kaṃsa</s> (<s>Kṛṣṇa</s>)
was a guest to the path of the discus's edge;
[<s>Bāṇa</s>], who from birth was inclined to devotion,
deserved protection but was not protected.
When <s>Kālayavana</s> arrived with speed,
<s>Śauri</s> (<s>Kṛṣṇa</s>) took refuge with <s>Mucukunda</s>,
his form contracted
upon the surface of the sleeping-couch.
When the head of <s>Śiśupāla</s> was cut off
by the discus of the discus-bearer (<s>Kṛṣṇa</s>),
no [eye] glanced toward the bows
of the kings who were his partisans.
The younger brother of <s>Duryodhana</s> was seen
with his blood being drunk by <s>Bhīma</s> —
[watched] by the weaponless women and
[the warriors] <s>Droṇa</s>, <s>Karṇa</s>, <s>Kṛpa</s>, and others.
<s>Vṛkodara</s> (<s>Bhīma</s>), his pair of arms constrained
by a vast python,
became loud-voiced with the sound
of his mother's compassionate cries.
Even of the great ones of old,
such was the ground of their intoxication;
who then approves of the boasting
of an ordinary person's unbridled valor?
Ferocity and cruelty toward the powerless,
steadfastness in grievous sins,
deceitful courage, and harshness of speech —
such is the valor of the base.
The valor of one who is cruel without cause
is called mere violence —
he who, like a serpent, is always ready
to take the lives of living beings.
This alone is the supreme valor —
the protection of others' lives;
a taker of life is no hero;
a hero is one who gives life to suppliants.
No virtue is gained by the valor
of one devoid of wisdom;
enraged by the rumbling of clouds,
the lion falls into a pit.
What use is the valor of a passionate,
intoxication-maddened elephant
that, out of greed for the lure of the tethering-post,
throws its body into a ditch?
What is remarkable about the valor
of a servant who has sold his body —
whose death, like that of a ram
tied in a slaughterhouse, is certain?
Those whose valor is not distorted by pride,
whose minds are not defiled by deceit,
whose learning is not heated by hatred —
their qualities are counted by the wise.
Just as family is destroyed by a bad son,
just as the rise of virtues by greed,
just as sovereignty by misgovernance —
so valor is destroyed by pride.
Like a pillar in the mansion of his might,
born of pride, there arose
a lord of the earth whose girdle-line
was the boundary of the seven oceans.
He, who had annihilated all enemies,
always longed in his heart for battle;
having found no rival to match him,
[this desire] became a thorn in his heart.
He, whose mind was made proud and haughty
by the pride gained from wars with gods and demons,
'Who, who is a hero?' — thus, in his fury,
he always asked the people.
To him — whose staff-like arms itched with pride —
as he asked impetuously,
girded for the contempt of all,
<s>Nārada</s>, having approached, spoke:
'There is no hero equal to you
in the three worlds — this is truly said;
however, I know two worthy of battle with you —
the sages <s>Nara</s> and <s>Nārāyaṇa</s>.
Dwelling at the <s>Badarī</s> hermitage,
established in fierce austerity —
if those two were desirous of battle,
then your heart's desire would be fulfilled.'
When <s>Nārada</s> had spoken thus,
he went to the <s>Badarī</s> hermitage,
gazing at his own arms,
[rejoicing that] the festival of battle was near.
Seeing those two treasuries of brilliance,
<s>Nara</s> and <s>Nārāyaṇa</s>, there, the king
arrogantly demanded the battle
he had rehearsed on the path of his fantasies.
Seeing him, eager for battle, with a sidelong,
deep, and steady gaze,
<s>Nara</s> spoke with a contemptuous
smile smeared on his lips:
'O king, turn back;
we are not skilled in battle.
Battle is fitting for you with those
who are your neighboring [rival] kings.'
Though told thus, when the king
would not budge from his eagerness for battle,
then [<s>Nara</s>] filled that arrogant one
with sharp arrows of <s>aiṣīka</s> (reed-shaft) missiles.
