His body covered with arrows
blazing like flames of fire,
the king, his bodily beauty destroyed,
abandoned his composure.
The king, whose burden of fierce
pride-fever was unexpectedly shattered,
pitiably, for the sake of saving his life,
sought refuge in that very [sage].
His weapons restrained by that one,
his proud heart's desire broken,
his throat choked with shame, the king
returned to his own capital.
Thus, even the pride of great ones,
being a terrible thunderbolt,
destroys splendor through pride,
just as iron is corroded by its own rust.
Therefore, a man who is rich in honor
should always strive to restrain his pride;
for the friends of one whose face is fierce with arrogance
are wholly ready for a terrible fall.
Heroes whose valor is free from pride, whose noble spirit is admirable,
who have worn away their own bodies in the protection of cows and <s>brāhmaṇas</s>,
attain immortality and agelessness
through their bodies of fame, moistened with the nectar of good deeds.
Sixth Inquiry
'In the world I alone, like a noble elephant with a path moistened by <s>dāna</s> (rut-fluid/generosity),
am the illustrious wish-fulfilling tree for the fruition of the hopes of the destitute' —

children.text: iti tyāgodagraṃ vahati kila darpaṃ manasi yas
children.translated_text: he who carries in his mind this pride, towering with generosity,
departs having destroyed all the merit that has arisen [from his giving].
From the desire for the fruit of enjoyment in heaven and such [rewards],
he who offers worship to a worthy recipient —
that is but a commercial transaction of buying and selling for <s>dharma</s>'s purpose;
what pride [is justified] by generosity arising from that?
That which is given to those who are gratified
by the particular excellence of qualities such as learning and the like,
from affection or from [desire for] wealth —
that is a [mere] commercial transaction of buying and selling.
He who gives with praises of [the recipient's] virtues
for the attainment of worldly renown —
he is making a commercial transaction
of wealth and fame at that time.
That wealth which is given
with contempt, struck by disrespect, without faith —
that is a barren seed cast upon salt-soil;
it is as if nothing was given at all.
That which is given in rivalry with another generous person,
from the desire to surpass [him] in fame —
is fruitful in the end only for the one
who was the [original] cause [of the giving].
Wealth [given] for the relief of others' suffering,
unannounced, unproclaimed,
given without expectation of fruit —
even a little attains the status of being much.
In places like <s>Kurukṣetra</s> and the like,
at times such as solar eclipses and the like,
merely for one's own benefit,
to a worthy recipient — what pride is there in such giving?
Without considering place, time,
rite, or recipient — simply
the alleviation of others' suffering,
given with a heart moist with compassion — that is called [true] giving.
'O son, for the protection of possessions,
for the attainment of a wife's happiness,
what is given with effort —
what [merit is there] in that giving born of greed?'
That which is given only after making [the recipient] a villain through debate,
through piercing, hasty examination —
long tormented — what [merit is there]
in that harsh giving?
Passing over a worthy recipient who has come seeking,
and giving instead to a prosperous one after soliciting [his acceptance] —
what [merit is there] in that 'burnt giving,'
scorched by [the worthy one's] sighs?
When something else was promised first,
but something different and lesser is then given —
that which is faulty or unsuitable —
what [merit is there] in that fraudulent giving?
That which is given out of the obligation of long service,
grudgingly, from the hardship of greed, unwillingly,
without grace —
what [merit is there] in that forced giving?
That which is displayed with flowers, incense,
and <s>tilaka</s>-mark as an offering,
yet given in an extremely small and worthless [amount] —
what [merit is there] in that ostentatious giving?
When, having amassed a great load of goods,
and upon the calamity of kings, thieves, and the like,
one gives what is damaged and proclaims it loudly —
what [merit is there] in that thorn-like giving?
That which cannot be tasted, cannot be sold,
cannot be taken, is not desired,
and is given as utterly useless —
what [merit is there] in that barren giving?
That which, like a debt, must be long repaid,
is given merely by a verbal promise —
breeding constant hatred from ceaseless begging —
what [merit is there] in that 'beggable' giving?
When the full [amount is given] to one, and a trifle to another,
though both are of equal merit,
that which is made proud through partiality — from attachment
and hatred — what [merit is there] in that biased giving?
When creditors, kinsmen, and sons,
having received a meager share,
are perpetually vexed —
what [merit is there] in that quarrelsome giving?
That which neither alleviates the suffering of another
nor serves as a cause of merit for oneself —
that which is obtained [back] at a small price for what was given —
what [merit is there] in that paltry giving?
When adverse planets are in conjunction,
when the ripening of fate is exceedingly terrible,
that which is given for the pacification of faults —
what [merit is there] in that fear-driven giving?
When a dying man, having abandoned all hopes,
lying on his bed, gives —
with a mind that is already at the threshold of unconsciousness —
what [merit is there] in that deluded giving?
That which is given by one whose mind is
tormented by the thorn of grief from the separation of a loved one,
that which produces remorse afterward —
what [merit is there] in that tearful giving?
That which is given incidentally
to a family priest or teacher,
who performs rites of peace and benediction —
what [merit is there] in that wage-like giving?
That which is given without desire for fruit, which is appropriate, which consists of one's all,

children.text: nānyāyena yadarjitaṃ paradhanasparśena śaptaṃ na yat
children.translated_text: which was not earned through injustice, which is not cursed by contact with others' wealth,

children.text: dattvā duḥkhaśataṃ na yatsvavacasā paścānna yadgaṇyate
children.translated_text: which does not produce a hundred sufferings when given, which is not afterward counted by one's own words —
that is [true] giving; the rest is [mere] skilled sowing of the seed of wealth — a method of cultivation.
Given for the sake of obtaining the pleasure of touching the breasts of heavenly women — a joy surpassing [earthly pleasures] —
even <s>Meru</s> [mountain], when given with the desire for self-benefit, dwindles to a blade of grass;
but when, upon witnessing the suffering of the afflicted, with compassion, filled with the nectar of faith,
accompanied by courage and enthusiasm — even a blade of grass exceeds the gift of the three worlds.
Of <s>Yudhiṣṭhira</s>, the earth-bearing king,
who rained gold in former times,
when the great sacrifice of the <s>Aśvamedha</s> (horse sacrifice)
was being conducted according to ritual —
when the royal feasts were prepared
in various rows of food-vessels,
and the twice-born were constantly eating
from gem-studded bowls —
while the <s>brāhmaṇas</s> were being filled
with awards of jewels and gold,
<s>Nakula</s> (a mongoose) came to the place of leftover food
from its burrow.
Adorned on one side
with a color of blazing gold,
and on the other with a dull color —
it aroused the curiosity of the givers [present].
It quickly approached the water
that had fallen from the golden vessels of leftovers
and rolled about with the tossing and turning
motions of a leaping fish.
The mongoose with its golden side
seeing [him] out of curiosity,
wallowing in the leftover water,
reported [him] to the king.
Having arrived, the king saw him and,
as if asked by a glance of longing,
he spoke with a voice
born of wonder, with clearly distinct syllables:
'O king, I do not see a fitting fruit
of this excessive giving.
From this abundant provision,
a [humble] vessel of barley-flour is far superior.'
'When this great giving proceeds,
O great king, in great wealth,
conduct, and mind —
who knows the purity in truth?'
'This provision, whose enjoyments suffice to pervade the dwelling of the world,
is utterly trifling in filling the extended multitudes in all directions.',
'In the method of pacifying the affliction of those in distress, in bestowing purity of character,
even a morsel of grass from those who are prepared attains the status of a mountain of gold.'
'Listen, O king, to what I myself have seen —
a wonder
at whose narration there arises
a coat of horripilation on the body.'
'Long ago, by a <s>brāhmaṇa</s> living by gleaning,
wandering through fields,
emaciated by fasting — though having a wife —
a small quantity of barley was obtained.'
'Then, when a vessel of barley-flour was prepared,
having performed the rites for the gods and ancestors,
dividing [it] into shares for wife and son,
he set out to eat his own portion.'
'He, desiring water for the oblation of the vital breath,
saw a guest who had arrived —
with a belly hollow from hunger,
with all limbs collapsed and limp in form.'
'Having offered hospitality to him
with a mind full of grace,
sprinkled with the nectar of faith,
he gave his own meal [to the guest].'
'When that was swallowed by the guest,
whose hunger-pangs were not diminished,
his wife too, with reverence,
gave her own food to him.'
'Seeing that even then [the guest was] unsatisfied,
their son, with faith in the guest,
with his own food brought about
the contentment of a full meal.'
'When the guest had eaten and departed,
the twice-born, emaciated by fasting,
endowed with courage of spirit, stood firm
through the night, exhausted yet free from pain.'
'Then I, drawn out from my burrow by the smell of barley-flour,
hungry,
reached his leaf-hut
where the discarded leftovers remained.'
'There, merely by the touch of the water
of [his] hand-rinsing, O king —
see my right side:
it has become golden in hue.'
'Thereafter, to obtain a golden hue
for my left side,
I have gone about sleepless with worry,
and have only become emaciated.'
'Whatever a man obtains
as his desire through the conjunction of <s>karma</s> (action),
he becomes subject to anxiety
for the fulfillment of exactly that.'
'Now, in this present
<s>aśvamedha</s> (horse-sacrifice) ritual of yours,
I have come with the hope of [attaining] a golden side
to the leftover-ground of the <s>brāhmaṇa</s>.'
'Though I have rolled for a long time
[in water] poured from vessels of jewels and gold,
not even a trace of luster
is seen anywhere on my body.'
'In every way, obeisance to giving
that is of the utmost purity of spirit,
extremely small [in quantity],
yet of great fruit — not to that which is an accessory to enjoyment.'
Having spoken thus, when the mongoose departed,
<s>Yudhiṣṭhira</s>, [thinking] 'so it is indeed,'
pondering with continuous sighs,
was stunned into stillness for a moment.
Therefore, one should not be proud
through gifts of gold, garments, jewels, and land.
Generous giving, with a spirit moist with compassion,
comes to someone only through merit.
Seventh Inquiry
<s>Tapas</s> (austerity) is always desired by the good
for the abandonment of pride in passion, wealth, and conceit,
and of delusion. If through that very [austerity] there is pride, then in vain
has the body been renounced and the body wasted.
With complete devotion and a purified mind, effort should be made
for the pacification of the faults of <s>saṃsāra</s> (worldly existence).
Austerity that is scorched by anger and smeared with attachment to wealth
does not produce keen tranquility.
If the mind is dispassionate — what use are austerities?
If the mind is passionate — what use are austerities?
If the mind is serene — what use are austerities?
If the mind is angry — what use are austerities?
Of sages whose lips quiver with curses due to anger,
whose lips tremble with desire,
whose sweat has a common origin [with that of passion] —
what use is the austerity of those who are without luster?
The wife of <s>Gautama</s>, <s>Ahalyā</s>, indeed
became a stone through his curse when he was angered.
King <s>Triśaṅku</s>, cursed in wrath by <s>Vasiṣṭha</s>,
was reduced to the state of a <s>caṇḍāla</s> (outcaste).
<s>Cyavana</s>, his form sunken in the earth, out of greed for precious jewels,
[endured] <s>Sukanyā</s> prying open his eyes,
[yet] out of regard for the pleasure of her hand's touch,
he, full of attachment, bore the injury.
<s>Pāṇḍu</s>, with his arms hanging around his beloved's neck,
departed, his body pressed against her breasts.
That <s>Parīkṣit</s> was burnt by the hissing of a serpent —
that was the manifestation of an ascetic's anger.
One by whom the very root of the tree of spreading <s>saṃsāra</s>
has not been completely uprooted —
what use is the false austerity of those sages
who are mighty in afflicting others with curses?
That which is not sullied by the dust of serving kings,
not heated by disputes over land or learning,
not troubled by the imposture of pretentious vows —
that pure observance is truly auspicious.
With hoarding, with wife and children kept hidden,
again taking up the burden of worldly affairs,
terrible with the pride born of pretension —
a false vow is [merely] a means of livelihood.
Afflicted with the disease of attachment, filled with abundant delusion,
with provisions for disease, with immense pride,
hot with the fault of hatred, with immeasurable deceit —
this foremost 'vow' bears the marks of <s>saṃsāra</s>.
Bound tightly by matted hair, rosaries, animal skins, yoga-straps,
and [obligations to] unmarried daughters,
devoid of discrimination, with the appearance of renunciation —
they call that vow a great bondage.
With a mind dyed in the saffron of passionate attachment,
or [one who is] sky-clad through the abandonment of virtuous garments,
whose heap of ashes is laughable due to fickleness —
a vow is not [true if it has] conduct equal to a bold costume.
Claiming the practice of non-attachment yet clinging to the enjoyment of wealth,
wearing a garland of dangling skulls,
agitated with anger, to be avoided by touch —
they call that burdensome 'vow' sinful.
A child as an ascetic — what is more laughable?
A youth seeking the forest — what is more unfitting?
An old man full of passion — what is more blameworthy?
A fool as a judge — what is more pitiable?
Forbearance, tranquility, mastery over the senses,
a mind irrigated with the nectar of compassion —
this austerity is worthy, whether in a community or in the forest.
The desiccation of the body, they say, is something else [entirely].
On the <s>Himālaya</s>, in a forest of dark <s>devadāru</s> (Himalayan cedar) trees,
beautiful with the smiles of waterfalls,
for sages devoted to the emaciation of austerity,
a time of a thousand years passed.
Then once, the Blessed One who removes the suffering of existence,
riding upon [his] bull through the path of the sky
together with <s>Bhavānī</s> (<s>Pārvatī</s>), for sport,
arrived — the one whose crest is the cool-rayed [moon].
Of his radiances that arose from his face,
extending the light of many moons,
by their playful laughter the sky became
[as if] clad in a white upper garment attached at the parting.
The Goddess, seeing the sages
reduced to mere skeletons by the intense exertion
of austere effort, her mind grieved with the onset of compassion,
spoke to [him] whose ornament is the crescent moon:
'O Lord, for these sages who are steadfast in your worship,
who have abandoned all attachment and restraint,
whose bodies are desiccated by the acts of austerity —
is there still no liberation? How wondrous!'
'Why do these [sages], fastened to suffering for thousands of years,
clinging to affliction, immersed in bodily emaciation,
not attain your state — that state free from disease
which leads to eternal bliss?'
'Broad favor toward newcomers,
indifference toward those long-established —
from the vast arrogance of capricious sport,
this is the easy nature of lords.'
Having heard the speech of his beloved,
full of affection, the Lord of the Mountain spoke to her,
making the luster of his poison-dark throat
surpassed by the radiance of his teeth:
'O Goddess, what you have said out of compassion for the sages —
it is fitting for me, in compliance with [my] devotees.',
'However, <s>kāma</s> (desire) and <s>kopa</s> (anger), which are the obstacles

children.text: śāntiṃ gatau kiṃ tu na kāmakopau
children.translated_text: to their transcendence of worldly existence, have not been pacified.'
'By forest-entries, by all [manner of] restraints,
by special rituals, by self-mortification —
they do not attain the state free from mental disturbance,
being dragged by anger and desire.'
'I shall directly demonstrate to them the disturbance
of [their] minds, clinging within.',
'By severe vows, only the body dries up,
not the dense delusion latent in [past-life] impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>).'
'Those who have abandoned enjoyments, freed from longing,
without passion even in affection, without attachment even toward the good,
devoted to effortless austerity —
they who are disciplined fully attain that imperishable state.'
Having spoken thus, <s>Śambhu</s> (<s>Śiva</s>), playfully
descending to the ground from [his] bull as if from a mountain-peak,
in an instant became a wondrous mass of beauty,
a naked ascetic, bright with the nectar of radiance.
His lotus-feet, as if moist
with the red radiance of the crest-jewels of the king of the gods,
inspired in the earth a marvelous pride
surpassing the fresh shoots of young coral creepers.
With clearly visible knees, thighs adorned with fullness,
a waist divided by the whirlpool-lake of the navel —
that form of his, with long arms,
had broad shoulders and a face [like] the full moon.
With limbs as if bathed in the midst
of an ocean of incomparable beauty-nectar, crystal-bright,
he made the ten directions widely luminous,
as if laughing at his sky-clad state.
His throat, dappled by the shadow-streaks of the dark peacock feather held in his hand, shone splendidly, like fire concealing the hidden <s>kālakūṭa</s> (poison) within, emitting a streak of smoke.
With two eyes, large-lashed
and charming with reddened edges,
he initiated, as if in a new union with the bodiless one (<s>Anaṅga</s>, the god of Love),
the consecration of passion in the women of the directions.
Seeing that body of the enemy of <s>Smara</s> (Love),
which aroused desire in all three worlds,
the third eye, ashamed by the memory of its former offense,
went somewhere [i.e., disappeared] for a moment.
He shone beautifully with a mass of curling dark hair
that touched his shoulders,
as if a host of [personified] nights had assembled
to search for the beloved crescent moon of his crown.
He shone with flowers, white as smiles,
released from the shoot-hands of the creeper-brides —
as if the daughter of <s>Jahnu</s> (<s>Gaṅgā</s>), concealed in another form,
[was present] with only the foam remaining, her hair scattered.
The new radiance he fashioned in another form,
to conceal his own true form, shone forth.
As if the moon, crushed from the matted locks by [his] hands,
was applied to all his limbs as anointing.
That form of the one who disfigured <s>Manmatha</s> (Love)
was [itself] ravishing through its radiance.
By it, a new desire mixed with wonder
arose from the stealing of modesty from the forest-goddesses.
Upon his unclothed body, [which invited] attachment,
the eyes of the <s>vidyādhara</s> (knowledge-bearing celestial) women,
who were modest, fell with longing alone,
half-concealed by playful lotuses.
For the celestial women standing in the sky,
subjugated by the beauty of his limbs,
whose ornaments jingled with trembling,
the feast of their eyes became an obstruction to their journey.
Upon his body, the multitude of gazes
of accomplished maidens appeared as if
clusters of blue lotus flowers released
from the tips of their cupped hands, stuck fast to [his] beauty.
Even for the doe-eyed [female deer],
motionless with curiosity at the sight of him,
who had made their eyes into ear-ornaments [i.e., looked with extreme attention],
there was an exceedingly eager stirring of the inner heart.
At his entrance, the creepers,
adorned with swarms of bees wandering in greed for the fragrance of his face,
agitated with yawning and sighing,
repeatedly trembled upon their blossoms.
Slowly, slowly, as [he], like youth itself embodied,
approached the vicinity of the hermitage,
the hearts of the sages' wives,
seeing [him] beautiful, leaped up with delight.
Their unblinking gaze, beholding him, entered as far as the ear-path [i.e., extended sideways]; having abandoned shame, with expansive desire, it displayed the grace of an innocent doe.
Of those [women] who had risen impetuously to worship [him],
whose garments had slipped, whose full breasts trembled,
who were subjugated by new desire —
the yawning became a graceful play of [their] arms.
On them, the line of body-hair appeared as if the beauty of darkness,
frightened by [their] moon-like faces, was guarded by [their] breasts,
as if the foremost streak of the spreading smoke of the fire of passion,
most delicate, issued from the navel.
Their gaze fell suddenly upon him —
as if eager for kissing upon his lip,
as if longing for forceful embrace upon his neck,
as if eager for the pressing of breasts upon his heart.
With [creeper-]blossoms in bloom whose outstretched smiles [were white],
with humming sounds [of bees] serving as rebuking cries,
with shoot-hands waved by the wind —
[the sages' wives] were as if being restrained by the flower-clusters [of the creepers].
As if threatened by the directions
through the frowning movement of brow-like streaks of sacrificial smoke,
they — ready to shed the silken garment of modesty —
shamelessly and forcibly became [enamored] in his presence.
Of those sighing women, trembling
as if by the breezes from the feathered shafts of <s>Smara</s>'s (the god of love's) arrows —
seeing their agitation of mind,
the assembly of sages became fierce with furrowed brows.
Their gaze suddenly became
like the twilight glow at the close of a day — as if spattered
with the blood of the doe of patience being torn apart
by the tiger of fierce anger — presaging the approach of the night of sin.
Biting their lips, swaying and reeling,
their bodies moist with sweat, breathing harshly —
those sages, jealousy rising with passion,
agitated with rage, assumed the very behavior of lustful men.
One, his waist bound with a black antelope skin
resembling the smoke of the fire of his inwardly blazing anger,
raising the triple staff, swiftly
rushed at the naked, bull-marked one (<s>Śiva</s>).
Another, with trembling arms, snatched up
a cushion and hurled it — devoid of patience —
whereupon [<s>Śiva</s>], as if from the separation from his seat (the earth),
quickly fell into a swoon, his body unsupported.
Another, seizing a water-pot —
resembling the mass of suddenly fierce,
accumulated rage —
in his delusion, stood ready to strike before the <s>Pināka</s>-bearing one (<s>Śiva</s>).
Of those who, from indignation, could not bear even a moment
to endure the affront, unable to tolerate [it] —
their prayer beads, fallen to the ground as they rushed forward,
assumed the furrowing [of brows] of that penance-grove.
From that commotion, a darkness resembling a great delusion
arose from the trembling flowers of the hermitage blossoms,
as bees — like the letters of a curse —
swarmed about, disturbed from within the petals.
Gazing at his face, moon-like, which was darkened
by the step of envy's word [upon it],
their eyes filled as if with the <s>kālakūṭa</s> (deadly poison)
of beholding his throat — they attained the swoon of delusion.
They — thirsting for the extraordinary excellence of his beauty,
the tip of his lip quivering with a smile —
spoke harsh rebukes, provoked by the agitation of their wives,
their syllables scattered by sighs caught in their throats:
'Who is this casteless, virtueless, yet accomplished one,
naked, bull-marked, entering shamelessly?
By whom this row of women — pure as
the <s>Gaṅgā</s> frequented by great sages — has been polluted!'
'By this one, indicating through his hidden
form, from pride, his low-born nature,
this hermitage ground of the sages has been reduced
to [the state of impurity caused by] a <s>kāpālika</s> (skull-bearing ascetic)!'
'Alas, the brilliance of this one,
who desires to embrace chaste women by force!
Surely by some magical trick of passion,
his form has been made handsome!'
Having spoken thus, in anger they hurled
upon him hundreds of staffs, stones, and cushions.
Delusion, born of the absence of discrimination
in those whose eyes are covered by hatred, becomes weighty in negligence.
When the moon-crested one (<s>Śiva</s>) had gone far away,
of those scorched by the vast fire of fierce rage,
the effort that had been directed to following the sight of him
turned entirely to restraining their womenfolk.
Then that blessed <s>Bharga</s> (<s>Śiva</s>), with laughter spreading
like the broad cascades of the celestial <s>Gaṅgā</s>, gradually vanished from that place,
and pervading the sky — tranquil and pure — said to his beloved,
her face white with a smile of amusement: 'O <s>Devī</s>, you have seen the conduct of the sages!'
'The body smeared with ashes, the mass of thick matted locks, the tonsure,
the bowl, the fondness for staff and water-pot, the holding of skin and prayer-beads,
the addiction to saffron robes, the delight in nakedness, the wearing of a garland of bones —
under the sway of desire and anger, every vow, however distinctive, is utterly vain!'
'From the rage of pride, from the binding of twisted matted locks in delusion,
from the inward sinking into clinging to the relish of juicy sense-pleasures,
from the mass of addictions to the noose of desire, from faults lurking in latent impressions —
for these, liberation does not come through austerity, through the mortification of the body!'

children.text: ityuktaṃ tripurāriṇā girisutā śrutvā yathārthaṃ vaco
children.translated_text: Thus spoke the enemy of <s>Tripura</s>; and the daughter of the mountain, hearing that truthful speech,
having determined that the vows of those whose minds are not at peace are merely a vain wasting of the body,
for the cessation of <s>saṃsāra</s>, for the pacification of the dust of delusion in sages, and
for the liberation from passion and hatred — with compassion she made her request to <s>Hara</s> (<s>Śiva</s>).
Then the blessed <s>Smarāri</s> (<s>Śiva</s>, the enemy of <s>Kāma</s>), entreated by the <s>Devī</s>,
with a compassionate glance of grace upon those sages,
his face bathing the quarters with a smile —
at once accomplished the pacification of the dust of delusion that had settled [upon them].
Therefore, through special austerities sharpened with effort,
let not the great pride of delusion be cultivated.
Through hatred, through passion, and through compassionless delusion,
austerity goes to ruin together with conceit.
When the fierce torment of inner craving is pacified by the waters of tranquility,
when the body is completely [refreshed] by drinking the spreading nectar of contentment,
when enjoyment is unattached — like a drop of water on a lotus petal —
in the forest of worldly existence, the generous austerity of men is indeed [the practice of] benefiting others.
